inline.s: Course
Textbook
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao-Qin [dynasty]

The Buddha-Treasure Sūtra, in three fascicles. The great master Kumārajīva translated this sūtra on the twelfth day of the sixth month of the seventh year of the Hongshi era of the Yao-Qin dynasty (405 CE). The whole sūtra is divided into ten chapters, discussing the reality of all dharmas as non-arising and non-ceasing, without characteristics and without activity. The reality of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still, is precisely the way of Buddhahood. It upbraids the various faults of a monk who has broken the precepts [saying] that he has ten arrows of sorrow and distress, and clearly sets forth the severe retribution — falling for long kalpas into hell — of those who preach the Dharma impurely and of the believers [who follow them], while [declaring that] “if a person, wishing to attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, preaches the Dharma for others, he gains immeasurable and boundless merit, and is also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.”

[Impure Dharma-teaching] To preach the Dharma with a mind of defilement — for the sake of fame, reputation, and gain — or to preach the Dharma without having properly understood the meaning and principle of the Buddha’s Dharma.

In studying and practicing the Buddha-Dharma, one must first possess right view. What is right view? To take the Buddha’s scriptures as one’s basis, to take the Buddha’s mind as one’s own mind, to take the Buddha’s words as one’s own words, to take the Buddha’s conduct as one’s own conduct — this is right view. For this reason, [I] have specially selected from the Buddha-Treasure Sūtra the “Reality of All Dharmas Chapter, the first,” the “Buddha-Remembrance Chapter, the second,” the “Dharma-Remembrance Chapter, the third,” the “Pure Dharma Chapter, the sixth,” the “Chapter of Ancient Times, the seventh,” and the “Chapter on the Precepts, the ninth,” and annotated them as follows.

The reality of all dharmas is the fundamental principle of Buddhism, and also the watershed dividing Buddhism from the non-Buddhists and from [the words of] Mara. The Dharma-Number Glossary of the Three Baskets says: “The various Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are all stamped and confirmed by the principle of reality. Non-Buddhists cannot mingle [with it], and heavenly Mara cannot destroy it. If it bears the seal of reality, then it is the Buddha’s speech; if it lacks the seal of reality, then it is Mara’s speech.” The Great Master Zhiyi, in the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra, says: “The various Hīnayāna sūtras, if confirmed by the three seals of impermanence, selflessness, and nirvāṇa, are the Buddha’s speech, and practicing them one attains the Way; without the three Dharma seals, they are Mara’s speech. Mahāyāna sūtras have but one Dharma seal, namely the reality of all dharmas; they are called sūtras of definitive meaning, through which one may attain the great Way. Without the seal of reality, they are Mara’s speech.” This sūtra takes the reality of all dharmas as its core, and is the most definitive and most ultimate sūtra; hence its title is “The Buddha-Treasure Sūtra.”

Since ancient times, philosophy in both East and West has been earnestly seeking the underlying substance of the myriad phenomena of the universe. But the Buddha Śākyamuni gave the correct answer more than two thousand years ago:
The underlying substance of the myriad phenomena of the universe is the reality of all dharmas.
Looking at modern science, the Buddha’s assertions are being confirmed one by one, ever more clearly revealing the Buddha’s great wisdom as ultimate and perfect.

blocks.text: 1. What Is the Reality of All Dharmas

inline.s: What is called “reality” (shíxiāng) is the actual state of affairs; “the reality of all dharmas” is the actual state of affairs of all dharmas. The Buddha-Treasure Sūtra says: “What is named the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing at all.” The Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: “All dharmas are alike in the characteristic of illusion; within them the Tathāgata, through the power of skill-in-means, is free of all defilement and attachment.” The Lotus Sūtra says: “The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as the reality [teaches], not inverted, not moving, not retreating, not turning.”

[Dharma (fa)] In Buddhist studies, “dharma” has several meanings: first, it refers to things and phenomena, including both material and mental; second, it means principle, rule; third, it means the path and Dharma — the principle, method, and stages of the path of cultivation; fourth, it is synonymous with the “Way”; fifth, it is the mental object (fǎchén), one of the six sense-dusts (form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and mental objects). Which meaning is intended must be judged from context. In “the reality of all dharmas,” “dharma” means things and phenomena. [All dharmas] refers to the myriad things and phenomena, the whole array of the universe.
[Empty] To have a characteristic yet no real substance (like the things of a dream) is called “empty.” In the Sūtra of Sustaining the World

the third chapter on the eighteen natures, the Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, without any root.” When describing the existence of things, besides “existence” and “non-existence,” there is also the case of illusion — for example the things of a dream, which do not really exist: they have a characteristic yet no real substance. To describe this, the concept “empty” is used. Master Hanshan says: “The Buddha’s word ‘empty’ is meant to break the attachment of worldly people who take [things] as truly existing; it is not the sense of utter nothingness and annihilation.” In the Vimalakīrti Sūtra

the third chapter on the disciples, it says: “All dharmas are ultimately without anything at all; this is the meaning of emptiness.” In this sentence, “all dharmas” says there is a characteristic [that appears], while “ultimately without anything at all” says there is truly nothing (ultimately speaking, there is nothing). This circumstance — having a characteristic yet truly having nothing (fantasy) — is called emptiness. Master Hanshan, on “emptiness is precisely illusion; illusion means having [appearance] yet not being real,” has a profound exposition, which I quote below:

Your letter seeking instruction is most sincere and earnest. But in what concerns the two words ‘empty’ and ‘illusion,’ you have not grasped them precisely (correctly), and so, with regard to mind and objects, you are not without obstruction, and hence your practice is hard. Now I will point [them] out to you, and then you will be clear and without the slightest doubt. What is called ‘empty’ is not the emptiness of utter non-existence; it is just like the common saying 'as if no one were there,' — but does 'as if no one were there' mean there is really no one? It is only that, raising one’s eyes, one does not see that person. What is called ‘illusion’ is not the illusion of strange transformations, but means having [appearance] yet not being real. It is like a peep-show in the marketplace, conjuring up all sorts of figures. Yet in that box there was originally nothing, and suddenly there they are; though they appear, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are originally nothing; and since they are originally nothing, we speak of ‘empty.’ Hence it is said: for example, a magically created person — it is not that there is no magically created person, but a magically created person is not a real person. Since the person is not real, is this not empty? The Buddha’s word ‘empty’ is meant to break the attachment of worldly people who take [things] as truly existing; it is not the sense of utter non-existence and annihilation. Truly fearing that worldly people would sink into annihilation, [he] further spoke the word ‘illusion’ in order to dispel that view of annihilation. Thus all body, mind, and dharmas: because of illusion they are empty, and because of emptiness they are spoken of as like illusion.” (The Collection of the Dream-Wandering Record
“Showing to Zhou Ziyin”)

[Peep-show] A wooden box containing a reel of pictures; at the front of the box is a row of small round holes (three or four), with a magnifying glass in each. After a customer pays, he puts his eye up to a hole and looks inside. The owner of the box slowly turns a handle on the side, and so one picture after another passes before the viewer’s eyes. Usually the pictures describe one story after another.

From this one can see that “empty” and “illusion” are synonyms. The Heart Sūtra says: “The bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, while practicing deeply the perfection of wisdom, perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, and passed beyond all suffering. Śāriputra! Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form. Form is precisely emptiness; emptiness is precisely form. So too with feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness.” In the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra

the eleventh chapter on the study of illusion, it says: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhūti said: No, Blessed One. … Form is not other than illusion; illusion is not other than form. Form is precisely illusion; illusion is precisely form. Blessed One, feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness are not other than illusion; illusion is not other than feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness. Consciousness is precisely illusion; illusion is precisely consciousness.” Comparing these two passages carefully, one realizes that “empty” means “illusion.”

The reality of all dharmas is the most ultimate truth, and so is called the truth of the ultimate meaning. But, just as when Copernicus announced that the earth revolves around the sun and not the sun around the earth, people found it truly hard to believe — and Bruno, for propagating this truth, was condemned as a heretic and burned to death — so too, in the Buddha-Treasure Sūtra

the first chapter on the reality of all dharmas, the Blessed One sets forth ten similes one after another to show how hard it is to bring people to believe and understand the truth of the reality of all dharmas. For example, one of the similes: “Śāriputra, suppose a person were to chew and swallow Mount Sumeru and cause it to be entirely consumed, and were to fly through empty space without finding it a trouble — what do you think, is that extraordinary? Extraordinary, Blessed One! Śāriputra, that all dharmas spoken of by the Buddhas are non-arising and non-ceasing, without characteristics and without activity, and [that] this brings people to believe and understand [it] — [this is] doubly extraordinary!”

Though it is harder to believe and understand, the reality of all dharmas is the truth — the supreme and highest truth. In the Lotus Sūtra, the Buddha says: “The Dharma achieved by the Buddha is the first, most extraordinary, and most difficult to understand, and only the Buddha and the Buddhas [together] can exhaustively know the reality of all dharmas.” Therefore, if one tries to deduce and ponder the reality of all dharmas with the wisdom of an ordinary person, it is like a firefly trying to burn Mount Sumeru — in the end it cannot. Hence the Buddha’s disciples should simply believe and accept the Buddha’s words and practice in accordance with the teaching!
Question: What is dharmahood (fǎxìng)?

Answer: Dharmahood is the essence (the underlying nature) of all dharmas, and is a different name for the reality of all dharmas. The Sūtra of the Buddha Teaching the Dharma of Kingship to King Sheng Guang says: “All dharmas, in their underlying nature, are empty and void, impermanent, decaying and destroyed. For example, a person, in a night dream, sees a fine garden, mountains and rivers, a throng of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and towers all delightful — and when he wakes up (waking from sleep), he sees nothing at all.” In the Great Accumulation of Jewels Sūtra

the sixty-fourth fascicle, it says: “Neither coming nor going, nor yet arising — the Buddha is able to proclaim such a Dharma; though [he] speaks of all dharmas as empty in underlying nature, the World-Hero causes [beings] to cultivate the Way.” The Moon-Lamp Samādhi Sūtra says: “The underlying nature of all dharmas is forever still; ordinary beings without wisdom cannot comprehend it. If one can abide the mind in stillness and concentration, that person has, always and everywhere, the Buddha.” In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra

the chapter on ascending Mount Sumeru, it says: “Dharmahood is originally empty and still; there is no grasping and no seeing.” The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Sentient beings and the world of lands share the same dharmahood.” The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: “Dharmahood is as previously explained: each dharma being empty, [they] are together one emptiness; this is dharmahood.”
Question: Since dharmahood is empty, doing good or doing evil should make no difference, right? Why, then, must we earnestly observe the five precepts and the ten good [deeds]?

Answer: Ultimately speaking, doing good or doing evil makes no difference, for both are the stuff of the dream of ignorance, both one emptiness. But while we are still in the dream of ignorance, doing good or doing evil makes a great difference: governed by the law of cause and effect, good brings good recompense and evil brings evil recompense, and suffering and bliss are plainly real, vividly true. Observing the precepts and cultivating [the path], we are precisely meant to awaken and remove confusion and inversion, and to wake from this dream of delusion.
Question: What is the Dharma-realm (fǎjiè)?

Answer: With regard to the phenomenal aspect, “Dharma” means all dharmas and “realm” means boundaries; all things in the phenomenal realm each have their differing and distinct characteristics, and cannot be confounded — this is called the “Dharma-realm of phenomena.” With regard to the principle aspect, although all dharmas differ vastly in their characteristics, they all share the same nature — this is called the “Dharma-realm of principle,” which is the reality of all dharmas.
Question: What is the One True Dharma-realm?
Answer: The One True Dharma-realm is the term used by the Huayan school for the ultimate principle, just as what the Tiantai school speaks of as the reality of all dharmas.
Question: What is dependent arising and the emptiness of nature?

Answer: Dependent arising says that all dharmas arise from the union of various conditions — this is spoken of from the phenomenal aspect. The emptiness of nature says that all dharmas, in their nature, are originally empty and do not truly exist — this is spoken of from the principle aspect.

blocks.text: 2. The Reality of All Dharmas Is the Fundamental Principle of Buddhism

inline.s: The one great matter of the Buddha’s appearing in the world is to lead all sentient beings to perfect the way of Buddhahood. The Buddha-Treasure Sūtra says: “The reality of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still, is precisely the way of Buddhahood.” In the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom
the fifth fascicle, it says: “Apart from the reality of all dharmas, all remaining dharmas are all called Mara.” In the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom
the tenth fascicle, it says: “The Buddhas of the three times all take the reality of all dharmas as their teacher.”
In the Lotus Sūtra, the Blessed One instructs: the three vehicles are expedient; the one vehicle is real. In the Lotus Sūtra

the chapter on expedient means, it says: “In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the one-vehicle Dharma — there is no second (meaning the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle) and no third (meaning the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva vehicles), apart from the Buddha’s expedient teaching.” “The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, through the power of skill-in-means, in the one Buddha-vehicle, separately speak of three.” “Only this one matter is real; the other two are not true.”

The three vehicles are the lesser vehicle (namely the Śrāvaka vehicle), the middle vehicle (namely the Pratyekabuddha vehicle), and the great vehicle (namely the Bodhisattva vehicle). The one vehicle is also called the one Buddha-vehicle, the sole teaching able to bring one to Buddhahood. The Śrāvaka vehicle practices according to the Four Noble Truths and so escapes birth and death; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle practices according to the twelve links of dependent origination and so escapes birth and death; the Bodhisattva vehicle practices according to the six perfections and so escapes birth and death; while the one Buddha-vehicle practices according to the reality of all dharmas and so perfectly completes the way of Buddhahood.

In the Buddha-Treasure Sūtra, the Blessed One gives a most detailed instruction on what the reality of all dharmas is, on its being the fundamental principle of Buddhism, and on how to cultivate according to it. Master Zhiyu’s
“Sketch of the Buddha-Treasure Sūtra”
, [has] annotated this sūtra very well.

blocks.text: 3. The Reality of All Dharmas Is the Truth of the Ultimate Meaning

inline.s: The reality of all dharmas is the truth of the ultimate meaning. The Buddha says: “All dharmas are all false; that place where they cease, this is called the real — this is called reality, this is called the Dharma-realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the truth of the ultimate meaning, called the ultimate emptiness.” (The Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra
the fortieth fascicle)
[Truth of the ultimate meaning] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth.
The Buddha says: “All dharmas are like illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage.” (The Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra
the tenth fascicle
the twenty-seventh chapter on Sadāprarudita)
The Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, without any root.” (The Sūtra of Sustaining the World
the third chapter on the eighteen natures)

The Buddha says: “All dharmas, in their underlying nature, are empty and void, impermanent, decaying and destroying. For example, a person in a night dream sees a fine garden, mountains and rivers, a throng of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and towers — all delightful. And when he wakes up (waking from sleep), he sees nothing at all.” (The Sūtra of the Buddha Teaching the Dharma of Kingship to King Sheng Guang)

The Buddha says: “In this there is no dharma that arises, and also no dharma that ceases; without arising, and without ceasing — this is the reality of all dharmas.” (The Great Accumulation of Jewels Sūtra
the seventy-seventh fascicle)
The Buddha says: “The bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas contemplate all dharmas and there is none that is not empty; this is the awareness of the reality of all dharmas.” (The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra
the five-hundred-and-thirty-seventh fascicle)

blocks.text: 4. The Reality of All Dharmas Is the One Dharma Seal

inline.s: A Dharma seal is the seal-contract of the Buddha-Dharma — the seal of truth handed down from Buddha to Buddha, the standard of Buddhism; whatever does not accord with the Dharma seal is not the Buddha-Dharma. The Hīnayāna Dharma is stamped and confirmed by the “three Dharma seals.” The three Dharma seals are: the seal of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, the seal of the selflessness of all dharmas, and the seal of nirvāṇa stillness. The impermanence of all conditioned phenomena means that all things in the world are at all times within arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing — what existed in the past has now changed; what exists now will in the end vanish. The selflessness of all dharmas means that all dharmas have no real substance. Nirvāṇa stillness means the realm of nirvāṇa, which extinguishes all the suffering of birth and death, unconditioned and peaceful — and so nirvāṇa is still.

The Mahāyāna Dharma is stamped and confirmed by the “seal of reality,” which is also called the seal of the reality of all dharmas. Since the reality of all dharmas already encompasses the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, the selflessness of all dharmas, and nirvāṇa stillness, it is called the one Dharma seal, or the one seal of reality. The Mahāyāna Dharma takes the exposition of the principle of the reality of all dharmas as its root; to speak the Dharma apart from the reality of all dharmas is all Mara’s speech. In the Lotus Sūtra, the Buddha says: “I, adorned with marks, my light shining on the world, honored by countless beings, speak for them the seal of reality.” The Dharma-Number Glossary of the Three Baskets says: “The various Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are all stamped and confirmed by the principle of reality. Non-Buddhists cannot mingle [with it], and heavenly Mara cannot destroy it. If it bears the seal of reality, then it is the Buddha’s speech; if it lacks the seal of reality, then it is Mara’s speech.” The Great Master Zhiyi, in the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra, says: “The various Hīnayāna sūtras, if confirmed by the three seals of impermanence, selflessness, and nirvāṇa, are the Buddha’s speech, and practicing them one attains the Way; without the three Dharma seals, they are Mara’s speech. Mahāyāna sūtras have but one Dharma seal, namely the reality of all dharmas; they are called sūtras of definitive meaning, through which one may attain the great Way. Without the seal of reality, they are Mara’s speech.” And in the Explanatory Notes on the Lotus Sūtra, [he] further says: “The Buddhas, awakening to the characteristic of reality, riding this real way, appear in the world. They only cause sentient beings to gain this reality; solely for this matter do they appear in the world, and never for any other. Apart from the reality of all dharmas, everything is wholly called Mara’s activity.”

In the scriptures and treatises one often meets the phrase “non-arising and non-ceasing,” yet it has two completely different meanings: first, the non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of by non-Buddhists means: it originally existed and is eternally present. Second, the non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma means: all things are illusory, and from the very beginning there was nothing (“originally not a single thing”), and since [they] did not arise, [they] do not cease. The Buddha says: “In this there is no dharma that arises, and also no dharma that ceases; without arising, and without ceasing — this is the reality of all dharmas.” (The Great Accumulation of Jewels Sūtra, the seventy-seventh fascicle)

In the Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, regarding the non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma, the Sixth Patriarch gave a brilliant exposition: “Xue Lin said: Master speaks of non-arising and non-ceasing — how is this different from the non-Buddhists? The Master (the Sixth Patriarch) said: The non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of by non-Buddhists is to use ceasing to stop arising, and to use arising to reveal ceasing; in that case ceasing is like non-ceasing, and arising, as it is spoken [of, is actually] non-arising. The non-arising and non-ceasing I speak of is that there was originally no arising, and now there is also no ceasing — and so it differs from the non-Buddhists.” (Translation: Xue Lin said: Master, when you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, what difference is there from the non-Buddhists? The Sixth Patriarch said: The non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of by non-Buddhists is to use ceasing to terminate arising and to use arising to reveal ceasing; in this way, ceasing is like non-ceasing, and arising, as it is spoken [of, is really] non-arising. Whereas the non-arising and non-ceasing I speak of is that there was originally not a single thing (“originally not a single thing”), and hence there is also no ceasing — and so it differs from the non-Buddhists.)

The non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma means: all dharmas never existed (originally there was no arising, hence also no ceasing) — this is precisely the reality of all dharmas (the actual state of affairs of all dharmas). In the Buddha-Treasure Sūtra

the second chapter on Buddha-remembrance, it says: “What is named the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing at all.” The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, in the midst of non-arising, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called turning in the wheel of birth and death.” The Sūtra of the Most Victorious King says: “Non-arising is real; arising is false and vain. Foolish people drift and sink in birth and death; the Tathāgata, his essence real, without falseness, is called nirvāṇa.” The Humane King Sūtra says: “All dharmas, in their nature, are truly empty, neither coming nor going, neither arising nor ceasing, the same as reality, equal to dharmahood.”
In the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra

the two-hundred-and-ninety-sixth fascicle, the Buddha says: “Good Manifest (Subhūti), in this great treasury of the perfection of wisdom, [it] does not speak of a single dharma as having arising or ceasing, defilement or purity, grasping or abandoning. Why? Because there is no single dharma that can arise or cease, be defiled or pure, be grasped or abandoned.” The Heart Sūtra says: “This is the empty characteristic of all dharmas: non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defiled, non-pure, non-increasing, non-decreasing.”

Therefore, the non-arising and non-ceasing spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma is the reality of all dharmas — originally not a single thing — how could there be any arising or ceasing to speak of? In the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra

the eleventh chapter on the study of illusion, it says: “The Buddha told Subhūti: What do you think? Does illusion have defilement or purity? No, Blessed One. Subhūti! What do you think? Does illusion have arising or ceasing? No, Blessed One.”
Question: Why is it said that “all dharmas are illusions”?

Answer: Because sentient beings are all in the dream of ignorance; all dharmas are the stuff of the dream of ignorance. All things in the universe are illusions produced by a single false stirring of thought, which lost the inherent nature. Master Yongjia’s Song of Enlightenment says: “In the dream, the six destinies are clearly there; after awakening, the great thousand are empty and nothing.”

In the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Blessed One instructs that sentient beings are in the dream of ignorance: “What is ignorance? Good man! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have manifold inversions — like a lost person who [mistakes] the four directions for one another — falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of self, and the shadow-images dependent on the six sense-dusts as the mark of the mind. Like one whose eyes are diseased seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky actually has no flowers; it is the sick one who falsely clings [to them]. Because of this false clinging, not only is he deluded about the self-nature of this emptiness, but he is also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, he turns in the wheel of birth and death — this is called ignorance. Good man! This ignorance has no real substance, like a person in a dream: while dreaming it is not nothing, but upon waking, nothing at all is obtained. Like the many flowers in the sky, which cease in the sky — one cannot say that there is a definite place where they cease. Why? Because there is no place where they arise. All sentient beings, in the midst of non-arising, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called turning in the wheel of birth and death.”

The Mahāyāna Esoteric and Adorned Sūtra says: “Like the colors in a dream (the form-dust — what is visible), existing only as false imaginative seeing, which upon waking is nothing. In the dream of ignorance one sees all sorts of forms, such as men and women; upon attaining right awakening, one sees nothing.”

The Sūtra of Divining the Karmic Retribution of Good and Evil says: “If, among such sentient beings, the perfuming of the Dharma-body has power, their afflictions gradually thin, they can tire of the world, seek the way of nirvāṇa, believe in and take refuge in the one reality, and practice the six perfections and all the factors of enlightenment — these are called bodhisattvas. If, among such bodhisattvas, the practice of all good dharmas is fulfilled and they ultimately attain release from the sleep of ignorance, they are then called Buddhas.” It also says: “All the practices of merit and virtue being fulfilled, therefore one becomes a Buddha — namely, abiding on the ultimate bodhisattva ground, able to remove all obstructions, because the dream of ignorance is exhausted.”

Master Hanshan says: “The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha, originally undefiled, without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the initial non-awareness, [they] delude the original self-nature — hence it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, [they] give rise to all sorts of delusions, manifold inversions, and create all sorts of karma, falsely taking the suffering of birth and death in the three realms upon themselves. All this is ignorance — not understanding one’s own mind, following the turn of delusion. Like a person fast asleep, having all sorts of evil dreams — all sorts of realms, all sorts of terrors, all kinds of suffering hard to bear. And when he wakes up, he seeks the events of the dream and cannot find them at all. For this reason sentient beings fall into the dream of ignorance, follow the inversions of delusion, create all sorts of karma, and themselves take up all sorts of suffering. Seen with awakened eyes, how could those inverted states be obtained?” (The Dream-Wandering Record
“Showing to Dong Zhiguang”)

[Three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. The realm of desire is the realm inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sexuality and food — from the six heavens of desire above, through humans and animals in the middle, down to hungry ghosts and hell below. The realm of form is the realm of beings who are without the two desires but still have a form-body — including the four dhyānas and eighteen heavens. The realm of formlessness is the realm of beings who have no form-body but abide mind-and-consciousness in deep, subtle dhyāna concentration — including the four formless heavens (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither-thinking-nor-non-thinking). These three realms are all the realms of the birth-and-death transmigration of ordinary beings; hence Buddhist practitioners first take escape from the three realms as their aim.
Master Hanshan says: “The Buddha said: All dharmas are like dreams and illusions. [He] also said: Birth and death and nirvāṇa are like yesterday’s dream.” (The Dream-Wandering Record
“Answering the Envoy Yuan Cangru”)
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra

the five-hundred-and-seventy-sixth fascicle, says: “If all beings could truly realize that all dharmas are like illusions and magical creations, they should originally have already realized supreme enlightenment; yet because sentient beings cannot penetrate [the fact] that all dharmas are like illusions, they transmigrate [in the wheel of] birth and death among the destinies.”

The Vaipulya Sūtra of the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata says: “All Tathāgatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish immeasurable power and divine might, and even realize the emptiness of all dharmas (all dharmas are illusions), being able to display manifold self-mastery in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. For example, a person dreams of all sorts of transformations, and when he wakes, everything seen is nothing. Ordinary beings are likewise: because of the dream of ignorance, they falsely give rise to the idea of real substance in all dharmas. The Buddhas, having awakened, all have nothing to which they cling, and so can, in a single thought, in all the worlds of the ten directions, display numberless Buddha-deeds, free and unobstructed, benefiting and perfecting all sentient beings, and causing them all to realize and enter the numberless deep and wondrous gates of liberation.”

All the above scriptures and treatises are saying: sentient beings are deluded in the dream of ignorance, inverted and transmigrating; while the Buddhas, the dream of ignorance exhausted, are free in the Dharma, and, pervading the worlds of the ten directions, display manifold Buddha-deeds to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
Master Hanshan, in the Dream-Wandering Record

“Answering the Envoy Yuan Cangru,” also says: “For bodhisattvas practicing [the path], even before the seventh ground, they have not yet broken the dream of ignorance. All along teaching sentient beings and perfecting the Pure Land are Buddha-deeds within a dream. Hence the bodhisattva of the eighth ground, [like] one crossing a river in a dream, is still not aware of it; only upon reaching Buddhahood is he called the Great Awakened One. This is stated in plain words, fully recorded in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra — clear and conclusive evidence.”

The dream of ignorance is a great dream, like a virtual world, in which very many dream-people interact with one another and can even build environments and objects. Yet people find it hard to believe that “we are in the dream of ignorance, and everything is an illusion”! This is not strange — if you have never awakened, how would you know that you are in a dream? Yet throughout the ages, countless people who have seen the nature and awakened [to] the mind have all confirmed: we are in the dream of ignorance. Master Yongjia’s Song of Enlightenment says: “In the dream, the six destinies are clearly there; after awakening, the great thousand are empty and nothing.” Through our own practice we can likewise confirm it — this is the reproducibility of science.

A dream, if you take it as real, enslaves you. Master Taixu says: “The mind in a dream is the mind of an ordinary person; the mind that knows it is dreaming while in the dream is the mind of a bodhisattva; the mind that awakens from the dream is the mind of a Buddha.” (The Outline of the Consciousness-Only Contemplation)

The Great Mahāyāna Compendium of Meanings says: “Buddha (fo) is a name established on the basis of virtue. Buddha means awareness and knowledge; on this [the title] is established. Awareness has two meanings: first, awareness of [defilements] is called awareness, as a person is aware of a thief. Second, awakening is called awareness, as a person wakes from sleep. The awareness [that is] awareness-of [defilements] is directed at the obstacle of afflictions; afflictions harm and bind like a thief, and only the noble ones, being aware of them, are not harmed by them — hence it is called awareness. The Nirvāṇa [Sūtra] says: As a person is aware of a thief and the thief can do nothing, so too the Buddha. The awareness [that is] awakening is directed at the obstacle to knowledge; ignorance is a dark and drowsy thing like sleep; when the noble wisdom arises, one is suddenly greatly awakened, like one who wakes from sleep — hence it is called awareness. Being able to awaken oneself, and also to awaken others, [with] the practice of awakening utterly fulfilled, [he] is called Buddha. Saying he awakens himself distinguishes him from the ordinary, [saying] he awakens others distinguishes him from the two vehicles, and the utter fulfillment of the practice of awakening distinguishes him from the bodhisattvas.”
Question: The great patriarchs and masters speak of a “dream within a dream” — what does this mean?

Answer: The dream of ignorance — this is the first word “dream.” Self-nature is the dreamer within the dream of ignorance, and self-nature falsely clings to the form-body as self and to the shadow-images of the six sense-dusts as the mind, and hence there is birth and death (the birth and death of successive portions), transmigration — this is the second word “dream,” which is to dream the dream of transmigration within the dream of ignorance. When afflictions are utterly cut off, one is released from the birth and death of successive portions and escapes the dream of transmigration; when ignorance is utterly cut off, one is released from the birth and death of transformation and escapes the dream of ignorance.

[Shadow-images of the six sense-dusts] These are the images that arise dependent on the six sense-dusts, namely the thoughts that arise when the six faculties meet the six sense-dusts. [The birth and death of successive portions] For sentient beings within the three realms and six destinies, because of [the karma] produced by good and evil deeds, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have distinct portions; hence their birth and death is called “the birth and death of successive portions.” One who has exhausted the birth and death of successive portions escapes transmigration and goes beyond the three realms. [The birth and death of transformation] The noble ones of the three vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and thought and exhausted the birth and death of successive portions, in the course of their practice have their delusive thoughts gradually extinguished and their realization gradually increase. This migration of delusion and realization differs from stage to stage; the transition from an earlier stage to a later one is like a passing through birth and death. Its transformation is wondrous and unfathomable, beyond thought — hence it is called “the birth and death of transformation.” One who has exhausted the birth and death of transformation perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question: It is said above that “all dharmas are illusions” — is the ālaya consciousness also an illusion?
Answer: Yes, the ālaya consciousness is an illusion. Because this question has always been quite controversial, I quote a few [passages] in brief:
In the Sūtra of the Undefiled [Vimalakīrti], the sixth fascicle, where it speaks of “no ālaya,” the Buddha says: “Though he delights in contemplating
no ālaya
, he does not abandon the treasury of the pure Dharma; though he contemplates all dharmas as ultimately non-arising, he always bears the burden of benefiting sentient beings.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the five-hundred-and-seventy-sixth fascicle, also speaks of “no ālaya.” Mañjuśrī (the bodhisattva Wenshushili) says: “All sentient beings may be established in the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma, in awareness and wisdom unmoved, knowing dharmahood to be empty, without name or characteristic, without support or abiding, without grasping or attachment, without obstruction or clinging, like empty space —
no ālaya

, no niryantī, no supreme stillness, the utmost stillness, non-arising and non-ceasing, undefiled and pure, unaccomplished and undestroyed, neither existing nor non-existing. Therefore, in this, one accomplishes the deep patience, always not far from the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma.”
[Niryantī (níyándǐ)] A different name for craving, meaning [that it is] utterly insatiable.
The above scriptures all say that the ālaya consciousness is not real — it is an illusion.

The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, in the Discourse on the Gate of the Hundred Dharmas of the Great Vehicle, classifies all dharmas into five great categories: the mind-dharmas, the mental-factors, the dharmas not concurrent with the mind, and the unconditioned dharmas. The ālaya consciousness belongs to the category of mind-dharmas among all dharmas. The Buddha says: “All dharmas are like illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage.” (The Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the tenth fascicle) The Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, without any root.” (The Sūtra of Sustaining the World, the third chapter on the eighteen natures) Since all dharmas are like illusions without reality, and the ālaya consciousness is one dharma among all dharmas, then of course it is like an illusion without reality.
